price.title: Price (Premium)
price.measures: The fair value of the option today under Black–Scholes–Merton.
price.intuition: Intrinsic value (how in-the-money you are, discounted) plus time value (the optionality). Always ≥ the discounted intrinsic; the gap is what you pay for convexity and the chance of finishing further ITM.
price.whenLarge: Highest for deep ITM and for long-dated / high-vol options. Time value peaks around the money.
price.desk: The number you quote. You make a two-way market around it: bid a bit below, offer a bit above, and manage the risk you are left with.

delta.title: Delta (Δ)
delta.measures: Sensitivity of the option price to a $1 move in spot — the hedge ratio.
delta.intuition: Call delta runs 0 → e^(−qT) (≈0 → 1); put delta runs −e^(−qT) → 0. ATM ≈ ±0.5. It is also a rough risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM. Buy a call → positive delta (long the market).
delta.whenLarge: Approaches ±1 deep ITM near expiry, ~0 deep OTM. The transition is sharpest ATM as T → 0 (that steepness IS gamma).
delta.desk: You hedge delta by trading the underlying (an index future proxy): short Δ units of the index against a long call to be delta-neutral, then re-hedge as Δ drifts.

gamma.title: Gamma (Γ)
gamma.measures: How fast delta itself changes as spot moves (convexity of the position).
gamma.intuition: Long options are long gamma (Γ ≥ 0): your delta grows as spot rises and shrinks as it falls, so a delta-hedge mechanically buys low and sells high. That re-hedging harvests realised volatility — paid for with theta.
gamma.whenLarge: Sharply peaked at-the-money and explodes as T → 0. A long-dated option has low, broad gamma; a 1-day ATM option has enormous gamma.
gamma.desk: Gamma scalping: long gamma + delta-hedging profits when realised vol beats the implied vol you paid. Near expiry, ATM gamma creates pin risk — delta whips between 0 and 1 around the strike.

vega.title: Vega (ν)
vega.measures: Sensitivity to a 1-point change in implied volatility.
vega.intuition: Long options are long vega (ν ≥ 0): higher implied vol → richer optionality → higher premium. Vega is the pure implied-vol exposure, independent of whether spot actually moves.
vega.whenLarge: Largest at-the-money and for LONG-dated options (vega scales with √T). Short-dated options have little vega but lots of gamma.
vega.desk: Vega is the implied-vol play. You express a view on the level of the vol surface (the VIX/VSTOXX gauge) with longer-dated structures; you warehouse vega and hedge it with other options, not the underlying.

theta.title: Theta (Θ)
theta.measures: Time decay — how much value the option loses as one calendar day passes.
theta.intuition: Long options usually have negative theta: optionality bleeds away as expiry approaches. It is the rent you pay to be long gamma. Reported per calendar day (the engine uses ∂/∂t = −∂/∂T).
theta.whenLarge: Most negative for at-the-money, short-dated options — exactly where gamma is largest. The two are locked together by the BSM PDE.
theta.desk: Theta vs gamma is the core trade-off: you collect/pay θ each day and earn/lose ½ΓS²·(realised² − implied²). Short-dated ATM = max theta and max gamma.

rho.title: Rho (ρ)
rho.measures: Sensitivity to a 1-point change in the risk-free rate.
rho.intuition: Calls are rho-positive, puts rho-negative (higher rates lift the forward). Usually the quietest greek for short-dated index options, but real for long-dated structures and for the carry (r − q) embedded in the forward.
rho.whenLarge: Grows with maturity and moneyness (scales with K·T·e^(−rT)). Matters for LEAPS and rate-sensitive books; small for weeklies.
rho.desk: Index desks watch rho mostly through the forward and the financing/dividend basis (r − q); pure rate risk is hedged with rates instruments when a long-dated book accumulates it.

vanna.title: Vanna
vanna.measures: Cross-greek: how delta moves when vol moves (= how vega moves when spot moves).
vanna.intuition: The link between spot risk and vol risk. Sign depends on moneyness (it flips through the money). With equity skew — where spot down tends to push vol up — vanna means your delta-hedge needs adjusting precisely when the market gaps.
vanna.whenLarge: Largest in the wings (away from ATM, where d2 is sizeable) and for shorter maturities. Zero where d2 = 0.
vanna.desk: Vanna is the heart of skew/risk-reversal trading. A risk reversal (long call vs short put) is essentially a vanna position — a bet on how the surface tilts as spot moves.

volga.title: Volga (Vomma)
volga.measures: Convexity in volatility — how vega changes as implied vol changes (vol-of-vol).
volga.intuition: Long volga = long the wings: strangles and far-OTM options gain vega as vol rises, so they benefit from an unstable, moving vol surface. It is exactly zero where d1·d2 = 0.
volga.whenLarge: Largest for out-of-the-money options (where d1·d2 is big); near zero around the money.
volga.desk: Volga prices the smile. A butterfly (long wings, short body) is a volga / vol-of-vol bet: it pays if implied vol is itself volatile.

charm.title: Charm (Delta Decay)
charm.measures: How delta drifts as one calendar day passes, with spot unchanged.
charm.intuition: Your hedge does not stand still in time: even on a flat day, delta moves. Charm tells you how much to re-hedge purely because the clock ticked.
charm.whenLarge: Largest for near-ATM options approaching expiry; notable across weekends (three days of decay at once).
charm.desk: Desks pre-hedge charm into Friday/over weekends and around expiry so they are not forced to chase a drifting delta on Monday.

speed.title: Speed
speed.measures: Third-order: how gamma changes as spot moves (∂Γ/∂S).
speed.intuition: The rate of change of your convexity. For a single vanilla it is small, but across a large book — or near barriers and on big gap moves — speed governs how quickly your gamma profile shifts under you.
speed.whenLarge: Largest near the money for short maturities, where gamma is most sharply peaked.
speed.desk: Watched on big or path-dependent books: when gamma is itself moving fast, a static delta/gamma hedge degrades quickly and must be refreshed.

color.title: Color (Gamma Decay)
color.measures: How gamma changes as one calendar day passes (∂Γ/∂t).
color.intuition: Gamma is not static in time: as expiry nears, an ATM option’s gamma concentrates and spikes, while away-from-money gamma fades. Color is that re-shaping of the gamma profile day by day.
color.whenLarge: Largest at-the-money close to expiry — the same region where pin risk lives.
color.desk: Tells you how your gamma (and therefore your scalping P&L and pin risk) will look tomorrow, so you can plan re-hedging into expiry.

keyRelationships.title: Gamma ↔ Theta (the BSM PDE)
keyRelationships.body: They are two sides of one coin: Θ + ½σ²S²Γ + (r−q)SΔ − rV = 0. A delta-hedged option’s P&L over a small step is ≈ ½·Γ·S²·((ΔS/S)² − σ²·dt) — i.e. ½·Γ·S²·(realised vol² − implied vol²). Long gamma makes money when the market moves MORE than the implied vol you paid in theta; it loses when the market is calmer than implied.

keyRelationships.title: Gamma vs Vega across maturities
keyRelationships.body: Short-dated options are a gamma / realised-vol play: huge gamma, tiny vega — you live or die on day-to-day moves. Long-dated options are a vega / implied-vol play: little gamma, lots of vega — you live or die on the level of the vol surface. The same volatility view is expressed with a different instrument depending on the horizon.

keyRelationships.title: Pin risk near expiry
keyRelationships.body: As T → 0, ATM gamma, charm and color all blow up. Delta snaps between 0 and 1 across the strike, so a tiny spot move flips your hedge from flat to fully long/short. Hedging becomes violent and expensive — that is pin risk, and it is why the acceptance test watches ATM gamma spike as T shrinks.

keyRelationships.title: Why the surface must move with spot
keyRelationships.body: Equity skew is real: spot down → vol up (the leverage effect). That co-movement is what makes vanna (∂Δ/∂σ) and volga bite — your delta-hedge has to change exactly when the market gaps and vol jumps. A static surface would make skew cosmetic and teach the wrong lessons; later phases evolve the whole surface with the simulated path.

call-vertical.name: call-vertical
call-vertical.view: Moderately bullish, with a budget. You want upside but refuse to pay full premium for an outright call.
call-vertical.structure: Long a lower-strike call, short a higher-strike call (same expiry). A debit spread.
call-vertical.greeks: Positive delta that fades to zero above the short strike (your upside is capped). Net vega and gamma are small — you sold most of the convexity back. Theta is mild.
call-vertical.risk: Defined: max loss = the net debit; max gain = the strike width − debit. You trade unlimited upside for a cheaper entry.

put-vertical.name: put-vertical
put-vertical.view: Moderately bearish with defined risk — the mirror of the bull call spread.
put-vertical.structure: Long a higher-strike put, short a lower-strike put (same expiry). A debit spread.
put-vertical.greeks: Negative delta that flattens below the short strike. Small net vega/gamma; the short leg finances the long. Mild theta.
put-vertical.risk: Defined: max loss = the net debit; max gain = the strike width − debit.

straddle.name: straddle
straddle.view: You expect a big move but not its direction — a bet that REALISED vol will beat the implied vol you pay.
straddle.structure: Long a call and a long put at the same (ATM) strike and expiry.
straddle.greeks: Delta ≈ 0 at the strike, long gamma and long vega (you own convexity and the vol level), and you pay for it with negative theta every day.
straddle.risk: Max loss = the premium paid, if spot pins the strike. The classic gamma-scalping / long-vol position.

strangle.name: strangle
strangle.view: A cheaper straddle: still a long-vol, big-move bet, but you need a LARGER move to pay off.
strangle.structure: Long an out-of-the-money put and a long out-of-the-money call (same expiry).
strangle.greeks: Delta ≈ 0 between the strikes, long gamma and long vega, negative theta. Less premium than a straddle, but a wider dead zone.
strangle.risk: Max loss = the premium paid, across the whole zone between the strikes.

risk-reversal.name: risk-reversal
risk-reversal.view: Bullish AND a pure SKEW bet. You sell the (expensive) downside put to fund the (cheaper) upside call — you are short skew.
risk-reversal.structure: Long an out-of-the-money call, short an out-of-the-money put. Often near-zero cost.
risk-reversal.greeks: Positive delta, and most importantly a big VANNA: with equity skew (spot down → vol up) your delta-hedge moves exactly when the market gaps. Low net premium but real tail risk.
risk-reversal.risk: The short put gives unlimited downside if the market sells off — you are paid the skew to take that risk.

butterfly.name: butterfly
butterfly.view: A pin / low-vol bet: you expect spot to sit near the body strike at expiry. A bet on the smile (vol-of-vol).
butterfly.structure: Long one wing, short two body, long the other wing (all calls or all puts), wings symmetric.
butterfly.greeks: Near the body you are short gamma and long theta (time works for you); cheap and defined. Sensitive to the curvature of the vol smile.
butterfly.risk: Defined: max loss = the small net debit; max gain peaks if spot lands exactly on the body strike at expiry.

iron-condor.name: iron-condor
iron-condor.view: Range-bound: you collect premium betting spot stays between the short strikes. A short-vol / income structure.
iron-condor.structure: Short a put spread below and short a call spread above (long wings further out). A net credit.
iron-condor.greeks: Short vega and short gamma with positive theta — you are paid to wait, and hurt by a big move in either direction.
iron-condor.risk: Defined: max gain = the credit; max loss = a wing width − credit if spot breaks through a short strike.

calendar.name: calendar
calendar.view: A TERM-STRUCTURE bet: sell rich front-month decay, own back-month vega. Profits if spot sits near the strike at the front expiry.
calendar.structure: Short the front-month option, long the back-month option at the same strike. A debit.
calendar.greeks: Long vega (the back month dominates) and positive theta (the front decays faster). Value peaks at the strike at the front expiry — hence the tent-shaped payoff.
calendar.risk: Max loss ≈ the debit. Hurt by a large spot move away from the strike, or by back-month implied vol falling.

digital.title: Digital (binary) option
digital.what: Pays a fixed cash amount if the underlying finishes beyond the strike — a bet on a LEVEL, not a magnitude. The building block of structured coupons (an autocall coupon is a digital).
digital.behaviour: A digital is the limit of an infinitely tight call spread: replicate it with (Q/Δ) call spreads of width Δ and let Δ → 0. Right at the strike near expiry, delta and gamma spike toward infinity — drag the spot across the strike and the payout flips from 0 to Q.
digital.risk: Un-hedgeable pin risk at expiry: an arbitrarily small move across the strike changes the payout by the full Q. Desks over-hedge with a FINITE call spread and charge the spread width as a cushion — you cannot hold the exact digital delta near expiry.

barrier.title: Barrier option
barrier.what: A vanilla that switches on (knock-in) or off (knock-out) if the underlying touches a barrier H. Cheaper than the vanilla — you give up the knocked-out states — so it is a popular way to cheapen a directional view. Closed-form under continuous monitoring; knock-in + knock-out = vanilla.
barrier.behaviour: Near the barrier a knock-out’s value and delta collapse toward zero, so GAMMA EXPLODES there: the hedge flips violently as spot approaches H. That barrier region is where a barrier book lives or dies.
barrier.risk: Barrier / gap risk: a jump through the barrier can leave you badly mis-hedged. The closed form assumes continuous monitoring; real contracts monitor discretely, which is worth a continuity correction (the price sits between the discrete and continuous values).

autocall.title: Autocallable (Phoenix)
autocall.what: A yield product: it pays periodic CONDITIONAL coupons and redeems early (autocalls) at par if the underlying is above the autocall barrier on an observation date. If it survives to maturity you are long the downside below a protection barrier.
autocall.behaviour: Path-dependent — the cashflows depend on the whole observation path, not just the final spot — so it is priced by Monte Carlo. The early-redemption probability and the EXPECTED LIFE matter as much as the price; the yield comes from an embedded short down-and-in put.
autocall.risk: You are effectively short a put: a sell-off below the protection barrier turns the coupon stream into a capital loss (par·S/S0). The greeks shift as spot approaches the autocall and coupon barriers — discontinuously around the autocall level.

varswap.title: Variance swap
varswap.what: Pays realised variance minus a fixed strike (the fair variance) — PURE exposure to realised volatility, with constant vega in variance terms and no path-dependent delta to manage.
varswap.behaviour: Its fair variance is model-free: replicate the log contract with a STATIC strip of OTM options weighted 1/K². The 1/K² weighting overweights low-strike puts, so with equity skew the fair vol prints ABOVE the ATM vol. VIX² is essentially the fair variance of a 30-day S&P variance swap.
varswap.risk: You own the whole smile: a jump or a spike in realised vol is your P&L. The replication needs a continuum of strikes, so wing liquidity and strike truncation cause real-world tracking error (and make a true var swap behave differently from a vol swap in a crash).

simConcepts.title: The market-making loop
simConcepts.body: A client asks for a price; you quote a two-way (bid/ask around fair); you win or lose the trade; you are left with risk; you hedge it; and at end-of-day you attribute your P&L. Every tick of this simulator is one turn of that loop — your job is to be paid for the risk you warehouse.

simConcepts.title: Spread vs fill — the edge tradeoff
simConcepts.body: A wider spread earns more edge per trade but wins less flow; a tighter spread wins more trades but is paid less for the risk. The skill is pricing tight enough to capture flow yet wide enough to be compensated — and skewing your quote when you already have a position you want to reduce.

simConcepts.title: Gamma scalping — realised vs implied
simConcepts.body: Once you hold an option and delta-hedge, your P&L per unit time is ≈ ½·Γ·S²·(σ_realised² − σ_implied²). Long gamma makes money when the market moves MORE than the vol you paid (realised > implied) and bleeds theta when it is calmer; short gamma is the reverse. The vol index (VIX/VSTOXX) is the implied gauge you are betting against.

simConcepts.title: The leverage effect bites twice
simConcepts.body: Spot down → vol up. So a sell-off hits a short-gamma / short-vega book twice: a gamma loss on the move AND a vega loss as implied vol spikes. The vanna term in your P&L explain is exactly this spot-vol interaction — it is why equity skew is not cosmetic.

simConcepts.title: Reading a P&L explain
simConcepts.body: Decompose each step into delta (spot × your net delta), gamma (convexity, ½Γ·ΔS²), theta (decay), vega (implied-vol move), vanna (spot-vol cross), volga (vol convexity) and a residual. A small residual means the second-order Taylor explains your day — you understand your risk. A large residual flags a gap, a big move, or risk you are not measuring.

attributionTerms.label: Delta
attributionTerms.note: Spot moved × your net delta (options + hedge). Hedge it to isolate vol/gamma.

attributionTerms.label: Gamma
attributionTerms.note: Convexity: ½·Γ·ΔS². Long gamma loves big moves; short gamma fears them.

attributionTerms.label: Theta
attributionTerms.note: Time decay — the rent you pay (long) or collect (short) for gamma.

attributionTerms.label: Vega
attributionTerms.note: Implied vol moved × your vega — the level of the surface.

attributionTerms.label: Vanna
attributionTerms.note: Spot–vol cross (ΔS×Δσ). Bites with skew / the leverage effect.

attributionTerms.label: Volga
attributionTerms.note: Vol convexity (½·volga·Δσ²) — the value of the wings.

attributionTerms.label: Residual
attributionTerms.note: What 2nd-order Taylor missed: 3rd-order, big gaps, vol-path. Large ⇒ look closer.
